Self-organizing workers share a Git repo, chat and a findings board, scaling from 1 to 1,024 agents on ProgramBench under a 6-hour budget. The post Microsoft Open-Sources Agensh: A Multi-Agent Harness for 1,024 Agents appeared first on MarkTechPost . ]]> Microsoft Research has open-sourced Agensh , a decentralized harness for large teams of coding agents. The Agensh multi-agent harness removes the central orchestrator that most agent frameworks depend on. Every worker picks its own sub-task, shares findings and merges code into a common Git repo. On ProgramBench, the team scaled the setup from 1 agent to 1,024 agents. TL;DR A Harness : Tested from 1 to 1,024 agents. Each worker gets a 272,000-token input and 128,000-token output limit. Runs on: Linux with Docker Compose. Single node by default (8 workers). The 1,024-agent run used 16 nodes, 64 agents each. Workers have a 64 GiB memory ceiling. Performance: more agents raised scores on all 5 hardest ProgramBench tasks, and reached them sooner. Best: 79.59% pandoc pass rate with 32 agents on GPT-6.1-sol. GPT-5.6-sol hit 55.06% with 1,024 agents. Worst: the 5-task mean reached only 28.78% at 128 agents. Going from 1 to 8 agents added 1.37 points. What is Agensh? Agensh is a multi-agent harness from Microsoft Research that coordinates many LLM agents without a lead agent. The target problem is the orchestrator ceiling. In orchestrator-worker designs, a lead agent plans, assigns and merges all work. The research paper cites Claude Code agent teams, Codex sub-agents, Copilot fleet and Kimi Agent Swarm as examples. Agensh lets the workers do that coordination themselves. How does the Agensh cooperation loop work? Each worker runs the same 5-step loop, concurrently and asynchronously: Gather context: read the goal, peer progress, messages and findings. Claim a sub-task: post a CLAIM, then settle overlaps by direct message. Take action: work locally with tools and post useful findings early. Verify results: check the work against the sub-task’s acceptance criteria. Merge progress: merge into the shared repo, post an update, then repeat. Three services connect the workers. Gitea hosts the shared workspace, with branches, PRs and merge conflicts. Mattermost carries a team channel plus direct messages for urgent collisions. A shared context board, adapted from DeLM , stores typed notes: OBSERVED, FACT, FAIL, CLAIM and PATCH_SUMMARY. The loop lives in the prompt, not in runtime code. Every worker gets the same prompt except its ID. Agensh sits on top of a single-agent harness. The experiments used GitHub Copilot CLI . The research paper states thin adapters can connect other harnesses, such as Claude Code. How well does Agensh scale on ProgramBench? Microsoft team tested the 5 hardest ProgramBench tasks: FFmpeg, gromacs, pandoc, PHP-src and ctags. Agents rebuild each program from its observed behavior. They work offline, within 6 hours. Reference repos range from 2,767 files (pandoc) to 26,266 files (PHP-src). With GPT-5.6-sol at high reasoning effort, the mean final test-pass rate moved as follows: 1 agent: 19.31% 8 agents: 20.68% 32 agents: 26.52% 128 agents: 28.78% That is a 9.47-point gain, about 49% relative. On pandoc alone, scores were 33.89% (1), 41.75% (8), 43.11% (32), 50.94% (128) and 55.06% (1,024). Speed improved too: on pandoc, 128 agents passed 30% at the 30-minute checkpoint. 32 and 8 agents needed 60 and 90 minutes. The README adds a newer model. With GPT-6.1-sol, pandoc rose from 56.19% (1 agent) to 79.59% (32 agents). That is a 41.64% relative gain. These GPT-6.1-sol figures are not in the v1 paper. What behaviors emerged as the team grew? The research team traced worker trajectories at each scale: 8 agents: peers agreed on interfaces and resolved overlapping claims themselves. 32 agents: peers reviewed shared work; one approval was withdrawn after a counterexample. 128 agents: workers reused trusted reviewers and standardized an integration protocol. 1,024 agents: several workers acted as integrators, and peers recovered failed work. None of these roles was hard-coded. How does Agensh compare with other multi-agent harnesses? Feature Agensh Claude Code agent teams Kimi Agent Swarm Copilot CLI /fleet Coordination No orchestrator; peers self-claim work Fixed lead session coordinates teammates Orchestrator decomposes tasks Copilot assigns parts to subagents Agents shown 1,024 tested No hard limit; 3 to 5 recommended Up to 100 sub-agents Not disclosed Shared state Gitea repo + shared context board Shared task list with file locking Not disclosed Plan from plan mode Messaging Mattermost channel + direct messages Mailbox messages between teammates Not disclosed Not disclosed Models Model agnostic; tested GPT-5.6-sol, GPT-6.1-sol Claude models Kimi K2.5 Not disclosed Speed claim 30% on pandoc at 30 min (128 agents) Not disclosed 4.5x faster than sequential (self-reported) Not disclosed Availability Open source, MIT In Claude Code; experimental, off by default Top-tier subscribers, research preview In Copilot CLI How do you run Agensh? The release includes a single-node Docker Compose team and a single-agent baseline. Both use native Copilot ACP sessions. You need Linux with Docker Engine, Compose v2, systemd, cgroup v2 and Python 3.11+. Defaults are 8 workers, 6 hours per task and gpt-5.6-sol at high effort. You also need ProgramBench (v1.2.5 was validated) and a model API token. Full steps sit in the reproduction guide . Key Takeaways Agensh coordinates up to 1,024 agents with no central orchestrator. Workers self-claim tasks via Gitea, Mattermost and a shared findings board. 128 agents lifted the 5-task ProgramBench mean from 19.31% to 28.78%. GPT-6.1-sol with 32 agents hit 79.59% on pandoc. Code is MIT licensed, but token cost is not disclosed. Check out the Paper , GitHub Repo and Project Page .
